rv.q: Clybourne Park is a powerful work about closed communities, exclusion and dehumanization of the other.
Clybourne Park proves itself more vital and relevant than ever on a big Broadway stage.
In Pam MacKinnon's expert staging, this is provocative entertainment that generates as much uneasiness as laughter.
'Clybourne Park' is everything you want in a play: Smart, witty, provocative and wonderfully acted.
Bruce Norris's brilliant, bracingly uncomfortable comedy about race and real estate in America has lost none of its sting in the move from off-Broadway to the Theatre.
If the walls in the modest bungalow in this ever-changing Chicago neighborhood could talk, they would be crabby. And why not?
The acting is searing, precise, and brutally incisive
That's a minor cavil about an excellent production of a great play.
His script is lean and mean and raises smart ideas about great divides between races, classes and sexes.
Thankfully, Pam MacKinnon's crackerjack production hasn't lost any of its punch since its 2010 premiere.
Few theatregoing experiences are as joyously liberating as being part of a packed house roaring with laughter at low comedy.

Observantly dressed by designer Ilona Somogyi, a well-meshed ensemble of seven excellent actors confidently invests their characters of 1959 and 2009 with distinctive personalities under director Pam MacKinnon’s discerning guidance. Designer Daniel Ostling provides a realistic setting that poignantly suffers the passing years.
Ultimately, it’s Norris’s play that lacks the Broadway curb appeal.

cn.t: Norris's Pulitzer-winning comedy about race and gentrification earns widespread praise for its sharp wit, provocative intelligence, and expert ensemble work, though it makes audiences squirm as much as it makes them laugh.
